The retrieved set contains mutually exclusive claims about whether alcohol literally kills brain cells. High-credibility sources d1 and d9 assert that alcohol can kill neurons or brain cells, while d2, d3, d4, d5, and d8 assert that alcohol does not kill brain cells but instead damages dendrites or interferes with neurogenesis. The short answer is that research is split: some credible sources say alcohol can literally kill brain cells, while others say it does not kill cells but impairs their function by damaging dendrites or interfering with neurogenesis. For example, one medical center states that alcohol kills brain cells and the damage may be permanent [d1], whereas multiple peer-reviewed and institutional sources argue that alcohol does not kill neurons but harms communication by damaging dendrites or reducing new cell formation [d2, d3, d4, d5, d8]. Some sources even claim alcohol can damage or kill neurons, citing brain shrinkage and memory loss [d9], while others attribute observed cell loss to thiamine deficiency rather than alcohol itself [d3, d5]. The disagreement reflects differing definitions of “killing” brain cells and the mechanisms by which alcohol harms the brain.
